what_it_is: A study of answer verifiers for RL with verifiable rewards in mathematics (p.1). On 8,000 responses from four math RL datasets, labelled by GPT-4o and checked against people on 1,000 (Cohen's kappa 0.93, F1 0.98, p.3), three rule-based verifiers reach precision above 99% but recall of about 86%, and their false negatives grow as the generating model gets stronger (p.1, p.3). Model-based verifiers recover many of these (recall 84% to 92% on Skywork-OR1, p.1). A hybrid that runs the rule-based verifier first and asks a model only about the responses the rules reject adds about 3 points of recall while keeping precision above 98% (p.4). In RL training, model-based verifiers, especially fine-tuned ones, can be hacked: the policy learns patterns (single words such as 'True', gibberish, prompt injections) that the verifier accepts, and scaling the verifier does not fix it (p.1-2, p.5-6).
domain: mathematical reasoning; similar phenomena reported for general science (p.2)
size: 8,000 labelled responses from four datasets; three rule-based and several model-based verifiers; GRPO training runs (p.3-6)
source_of_items: responses sampled from several models on existing math RL datasets (p.3)
evaluation: verifier precision and recall against labels; RL outcomes against oracle rewards; adversarial probing (p.3-6)
human_validation: GPT-4o's labels checked against human judgments on 1,000 examples: Cohen's kappa 0.93, F1 0.98 (p.3)

engtrace_use.sentence: Rule-based checkers avoid these biases but can reject correct answers given in unexpected formats [@huang2026verifierrobustness].
engtrace_use.explanation: The paper finds that rule-based verifiers 'fail to recognize equivalent answers in different formats, leading to substantial false negatives' (p.1), with precision above 99% (p.3). The sentence leaves out the paper's second result, which bears on EngTrace's design: the rule-first hybrid that sends only rule-rejected responses to a model is the pattern EngTrace's residual judge follows, and it improves recall at little cost to precision in static evaluation (p.4).

recommendation: keep as is; also cite in the appendix's sentence on escalation, for the rule-first hybrid
suggested_wording: Appendix: '@jung2025trustescalate escalate only uncertain items to stronger judges, and @huang2026verifierrobustness ask a model only about answers a rule-based verifier rejects, the pattern EngTrace's residual judge follows.'
facts_to_cite: rule-based verifiers fail to recognise equivalent answers in different formats; average recall about 86% (p.1)
rule-based verifiers have near-perfect precision, above 99% (p.3)
hybrid: the rule-based verifier first, the model only when the rules flag a response as incorrect; about 3 points more recall at more than 98% precision (p.4)
model-based verifiers are susceptible to reward hacking in RL, particularly after fine-tuning (p.1)
overlap_with_engtrace: Implications for EngTrace. (1) The deterministic answer check is exposed to the false negatives this paper measures; EngTrace measured them directly, against experts, rather than assuming them away (answer-check agreement 0.982 on 281 non-partial traces after D-137, evaluator_pilot_17092026/RESULTS_X1.md via the state brief, section 3). (2) The residual judge is this paper's hybrid design: the deterministic milestone check first, MiMo only on the milestones it missed (full_run_28092026/judge.py). The paper's evidence favours it in static evaluation. (3) Its hacking result concerns a policy trained against the verifier; EngTrace's models are not optimised against its judge, so the result does not transfer directly, but its probing shows model verifiers can accept assertions of correctness, which is a reason the judge's precision against experts (E5 milestone precision 0.930, recall 0.989, RESULTS_X1) belongs in the paper. No change to the positioning claim.
notes: (1) The venue rests on the arXiv comment alone. (2) The paper's verifiers judge final answers in mathematics; EngTrace's judge decides intermediate milestones against expected values, a narrower question.
